title: Review: Gravitational fields; Electric and magnetic fields

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Point mass
items.clue: An idealised body whose size and shape play no part.

items.label: Kepler's first law
items.clue: Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus.

items.label: Electric field strength
items.clue: The force per unit charge on a small positive test charge.

items.label: Neutral point
items.clue: Where the resultant of two or more charges' fields is zero.

questions.stem: Io and Europa are moons of Jupiter, and their orbits may be taken as circular. Io has an orbital radius of 4.22 × 10⁸ m and a time period of 1.77 days. Europa has an orbital radius of 6.71 × 10⁸ m. What is the time period of Europa?

options.text: 2.81 days
3.55 days
1.77 days
4.48 days

questions.explanation: By Kepler's third law T² ∝ r³ for moons of the same planet, so T_E = T_I × (r_E/r_I)^(3/2) = 1.77 × (6.71/4.22)^(3/2) = 1.77 × 2.005 = 3.55 days.

questions.stem: A satellite of mass 1200 kg orbits the Earth at a height of 600 km above the surface. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6370 km. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational force that the Earth exerts on the satellite?
questions.explanation: r is measured from the Earth's centre: r = 6370 km + 600 km = 6970 km = 6.97 × 10⁶ m. F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 1200 / (6.97 × 10⁶)² = 9.84 × 10³ N.

questions.stem: A planet is a sphere of uniform density. Why can it be treated as a point mass at its centre when calculating the gravitational force on a satellite orbiting it?

options.text: A satellite is usually far away compared with the planet's radius, so the planet looks like a point.
The satellite's mass is tiny compared with the planet's, so the planet's size is irrelevant.
All of the planet's mass is concentrated at its centre, where its gravity comes from.
At any point outside a uniform sphere, its field is that of a point mass at its centre.

questions.stem: At the surface of the Earth, g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Planet X has the same mass as the Earth but half its radius. Both may be treated as uniform spheres. What is the gravitational field strength at the surface of planet X?

options.text: 39.2 N kg⁻¹
19.6 N kg⁻¹
9.80 N kg⁻¹
4.90 N kg⁻¹

questions.explanation: g = GM/R². With the same M and half the R, g increases by a factor 1/(0.5)² = 4: 4 × 9.8 = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.

questions.stem: Close to the surface of a planet, over a region a few kilometres across, the gravitational field is drawn as parallel, equally spaced field lines pointing vertically downwards. What does this pattern show about the field in that region?

options.text: Any object released or thrown in the region moves along one of the field lines.
The field acts only along the lines drawn, with no field in the gaps between them.
The field strength has the same size and direction at every point in the region.
A heavier object placed in the region experiences a larger field strength.

questions.explanation: Parallel lines show the same direction everywhere, and equal spacing shows the same strength everywhere: a uniform field. This is the assumed uniform field close to the surface of a planet.

questions.stem: Point charges +Q and −Q are fixed a distance 2d apart. A small positively charged ball is released from rest at the midpoint between them. Which statement about the electric force on the ball at the moment of release is correct?

options.text: It is zero, since the ball is the same distance from the two fixed charges and so their forces on it cancel out.
It is zero, since the fixed charges add up to no net charge and so together they exert no force at all on the ball.
It is directed towards −Q, since it is pushed away from +Q and pulled towards −Q, both forces acting one way.
It is directed towards +Q, since it is pulled towards +Q and pushed away from −Q, both forces acting the same way in that direction.

questions.stem: Two small insulating spheres, each of diameter 2.0 cm, carry charges of +10 nC and +15 nC spread uniformly over them. They are in a vacuum with a gap of 3.0 cm between their surfaces. Take k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the magnitude of the electric force between them?
questions.explanation: Each uniformly charged sphere acts as a point charge at its centre, so r = 1.0 cm + 3.0 cm + 1.0 cm = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m. F = kq₁q₂/r² = 8.99 × 10⁹ × 10 × 10⁻⁹ × 15 × 10⁻⁹/(0.050)² = 5.4 × 10⁻⁴ N.

questions.stem: A polythene rod is rubbed with a dry woollen cloth and gains a charge of −8.0 nC. Which statement about the cloth after the rubbing is correct?

options.text: Its charge is −8.0 nC, because rubbing charges both surfaces in the same way.
Its charge is +8.0 nC, as the electrons the rod gained came from the cloth.
It is uncharged, because the friction created the charge on the rod alone.
Its charge is +8.0 nC, because protons moved from the rod to the cloth.

questions.explanation: Charge is conserved. The rod became negative by gaining electrons, and the only place they came from is the cloth, which is left short of the same number of electrons: +8.0 nC.

questions.stem: Kepler's third law describes the orbits of the planets around the Sun. Taking each orbit as a circle of radius r with time period T, which statement expresses the law?

options.text: T/r has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
T has the same value for every planet, whatever its distance.
T²/r³ has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
T²/r³ has one value for all orbiting bodies, whatever they orbit.

questions.explanation: This is Kepler's third law, T² ∝ r³. For circular orbits it follows from GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r, which gives T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, the same for every planet because M is the Sun's mass.

questions.stem: The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?

options.text: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
It is zero, as the Moon has no air and so has no gravity.

questions.explanation: The two forces are a Newton's third law pair: equal in size, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² contains the product of both masses, so the same value applies to each body. The force on the Earth points towards the Moon.

questions.stem: Which statement defines the gravitational field strength g at a point?

options.text: The gravitational force acting on any object placed at that point, in newtons.
The gravitational force per unit mass on a small point mass placed at that point.
The acceleration of free fall at that point, which is 9.8 m s⁻² at every point.
The force per unit mass on a small point mass, directed away from the mass producing the field.

questions.explanation: This is the definition in the guide: g = F/m for a small test mass, one small enough not to disturb the field. The unit is N kg⁻¹, equivalent to m s⁻².

questions.stem: A student sketches the gravitational field lines around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere. Which description of a correct sketch is right?

options.text: Straight radial lines pointing inwards to the planet's centre, closer together near its surface.
Straight radial lines pointing outwards from the planet's centre, closer together near it.
Parallel lines all pointing 'down' in one direction, equally spaced at all distances.
Curved lines that leave the planet near one pole and re-enter it near the other.

questions.stem: A probe of mass m is lifted from the surface of a planet of radius R to a height R above the surface. The field strength at the surface is g. A student calculates the gain in gravitational potential energy using ΔE_p = mgΔh with Δh = R. How does the student's answer compare with the true gain, found from E_p = −GMm/r?

options.text: 1.0 times the true gain
4.0 times the true gain
1.6 times the true gain
2.0 times the true gain

questions.explanation: True gain: GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/2R. Since g = GM/R², GMm/2R = ½mgR. The student's mgR is therefore 2.0 times the true gain, because g falls as the probe rises and less work is needed for each metre higher up.

questions.stem: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational potential due to the Moon at a point 1.00 × 10⁶ m above its surface?

A graph shows the gravitational potential V_g along a radial line from the centre of a planet, plotted against the distance r from the centre. Which statement about the gravitational field strength g at a point outside the planet on this line is correct?

options.text: g is the gradient of the graph at that point, so the field is directed towards higher V_g, outwards.
g is fixed by the value of V_g at that point alone, and does not depend on how V_g changes with r near the point.
g is minus the gradient of the graph at that point, so the field is directed towards lower V_g.
g is zero at that point whenever the point lies on an equipotential surface, however steep the graph is there.

questions.stem: An 800 kg satellite is launched from rest on the surface of a non-rotating planet of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and placed in a circular orbit of radius 1.00 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Ignoring air resistance, what is the minimum energy that must be supplied to the satellite?
questions.explanation: Energy supplied = E_total in orbit − E_p at surface = −GMm/2r − (−GMm/R) = 3.186 × 10¹⁷ × (1/6.37 × 10⁶ − 1/2.00 × 10⁷) = 5.001 × 10¹⁰ − 1.593 × 10¹⁰ = 3.41 × 10¹⁰ J.

questions.stem: The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and the gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². An equipotential surface around the Earth has gravitational potential V_g = −2.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. What is the radius of this surface, measured from the centre of the Earth?
questions.explanation: An equipotential around a spherical mass is a sphere on which V_g = −GM/r has one value, so r = GM/|V_g| = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴)/(2.50 × 10⁷) = 1.59 × 10⁷ m, measured from the centre.

questions.stem: A small mass is moved along an equipotential surface in a gravitational field. Which statement is correct?

options.text: There is no gravitational field on the surface, so no force acts on the mass.
Gravity does work on the mass, as its weight acts on it all the time it moves.
The field acts along the surface, in the same direction as the mass moves.
The field is perpendicular to its path, so gravity does no work on the mass.

questions.explanation: Field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, so the gravitational force has no component along the path. With W = mΔV_g and ΔV_g = 0, no work is done by gravity.
